synopsis: MOSH supplies an engineering compliance route for South African mining collision prevention, combining industry performance requirements with supplier and independent physical verification at TRL gates, rather than treating regulatory wording as a complete specification [f1855, f2478, f2593]. Its surface requirements include 200 m detection, warning 2.5–3.0 seconds before intervention, fail-to-safe within 500 ms of detecting a critical failure, disconnection detection within 500 ms, and machine replies within 50 ms [f174, f175, f2359, f5284, f5285]. Emergency-stop deceleration is specified as 1.9 m/s² for machines with top speeds above 20 km/h and 1.0 m/s² otherwise; stopping performance also depends on gradient, side slope and braking response [f5560, f3401]. University of Pretoria testing reported pass rates of 62% for detection devices, 42% for machine-side systems and 83% for third-party interfaces across 189 tests, with throughput of 1.6 tests per week and an 18-week lead time as of October 2025 [f5178, f5180]. Verification must separately cover machines with different braking characteristics, yet published stopping tests cover only unloaded machines on gradients of 1% or less, limiting the demonstrated operating envelope [f5181, f5182]. MOSH requires no false interventions at TRL4, while its 2022 guidance warns that nuisance interventions and fixed stop gaps can disrupt production or loading enough to prompt switching systems off; the glossary also leaves a timing ambiguity by describing both failure detection and reaching a safe state within 500 ms, versus the specification's interval after critical-failure detection [f178, f3300, f3344, f12132, f2359].
